(5) A cached empowerment landscape, ℰ̂(s)\hat{\mathcal{E}}(s). Computing empowerment from scratch at every encountered state via forward-model rollout and channel-capacity optimization is computationally prohibitive for real-time decision-making. A more plausible architecture maintains a learned value map ℰ̂:𝒮→ℝ\hat{\mathcal{E}}: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} that caches empowerment estimates across the state space, updated incrementally as the agent explores and refines its forward model. This cached landscape then serves as a pseudo-reward or intrinsic value function that can be queried rapidly during action selection: the agent can evaluate candidate next states by looking up ℰ̂(s′)\hat{\mathcal{E}}(s') rather than re-solving the channel-capacity problem de novo. Such a representation is analogous to the successor representation (SR) 1, which caches expected future state occupancy. Just as the SR allows rapid recomputation of value under changing reward functions by separating "what states will I visit?" from "how rewarding are they?," a cached empowerment map separates "how controllable is this region?" from the current goal, enabling the agent to navigate toward high-empowerment states as a background policy even when the primary objective is defined by other terms (e.g., EFE risk minimization). Maintaining this landscape requires ongoing calibration: as the agent’s motor skills improve (expanding the action repertoire) or as the environment changes (altering transition dynamics), previously cached ℰ̂\hat{\mathcal{E}} values become stale, necessitating a mechanism for empowerment prediction errors–discrepancies between expected and experienced controllability–that trigger local re-estimation, much as reward prediction errors trigger value function updates in temporal-difference learning.

Neural architecture; how is it evolutionarily instantiated as an architectural prior?

The neural substrate for a cached empowerment landscape requires three things: (i) a state-indexed memory that covers the environment and supports smooth generalization to unvisited states, (ii) a mechanism for associating controllability values with state representations, and (iii) a prediction-error signal for incremental re-estimation when cached values become stale.

The hippocampal-entorhinal system provides a natural scaffold for (i). Beyond encoding a cognitive map, hippocampal place-cell representations exhibit properties consistent with the successor representation (SR): place fields are distorted by transition statistics under the agent’s policy, encoding expected future state occupancy rather than mere location 2. This is significant because the SR at state ss implicitly encodes reachability structure–the diversity, depth, and probability of states accessible from ss under the current policy–which is precisely the substrate from which empowerment can be read. The rank and entropy of the SR row vector at ss reflect how many distinct futures the agent’s policy explores from that state; regions of state space with high-rank, high-entropy SR rows are exactly the high-empowerment regions. Grid cells in entorhinal cortex supply a multi-scale periodic basis set whose spatial frequencies correspond to eigenvectors of the SR 2, 3, providing a compressed, smoothly interpolable representation that enables generalization of cached ℰ̂\hat{\mathcal{E}} to states the agent has never physically occupied–the neural analogue of function approximation over a continuous value landscape. The network schematic makes the place-to-grid transformation explicit (Figure). The model outputs show the effect of the non-negative-weight constraint (Figure).

For (ii), the hippocampal formation projects densely to ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) and to orbitofrontal / ventromedial prefrontal cortex–regions canonically associated with state-value representation and model-based evaluation 4, 5. These projections supply the anatomical pathway for linking state representations to cached empowerment estimates: ventral striatum can store ℰ̂(s)\hat{\mathcal{E}}(s) as a pseudo-reward value function via standard dopaminergic TD learning (see “Neuromodulators”), while OFC/vmPFC can maintain a more flexible, model-based empowerment estimate that updates when the agent’s world model is revised (e.g., after discovering that a door is now locked). The convergence of hippocampal state representations and midbrain dopaminergic teaching signals onto striatal medium spiny neurons is a phylogenetically ancient wiring motif, conserved across amniotes, that evolution has repurposed for caching many forms of state value–empowerment included.

Maintaining ℰ̂\hat{\mathcal{E}} across a large state space requires offline propagation to states the agent has not recently visited. Hippocampal sharp-wave ripple (SWR)-associated replay provides exactly this: compressed reactivation of trajectory sequences during rest and sleep drives simulated “experience” at distant states, enabling TD-like updates to propagate empowerment estimates across the cognitive map without physical traversal 6, 7. Evidence that replay is prioritized toward trajectories with large unsigned prediction errors or high information gain 7 suggests a natural mechanism for concentrating ℰ̂\hat{\mathcal{E}} re-estimation on regions where cached controllability values are most likely stale–e.g., near recently changed environmental affordances or newly acquired motor skills.

For (iii), the empowerment prediction error–the discrepancy between cached ℰ̂(s)\hat{\mathcal{E}}(s) and controllability as actually experienced upon arrival–can be carried by dopaminergic RPE signals if empowerment contributes to intrinsic value (see bullet 1 above). But a more specific controllability-monitoring circuit exists in medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly prelimbic / anterior cingulate regions. Maier and Seligman’s revised learned-helplessness model argues that mPFC actively detects when outcomes are controllable (instrumentally contingent on actions) and, upon such detection, inhibits default passivity and anxiety-like responses originating from dorsal raphe serotonergic projections and amygdala 8. This mPFC circuit is functionally a controllability monitor: it signals whether the current state affords causal influence, which is exactly what empowerment measures. Discrepancies between mPFC’s real-time controllability assessment and the cached landscape value could thus serve as the trigger for re-estimation of ℰ̂\hat{\mathcal{E}} in the relevant region of state space, analogous to how RPEs trigger value-function updates in reward-based TD learning.

The evolutionary architectural priors are therefore: (i) the hippocampal-entorhinal cognitive map (place cells, grid cells, boundary cells) supplying a structured, SR-like state scaffold over which controllability values can be smoothly cached and generalized; (ii) the hippocampal→\rightarrowventral striatum and hippocampal→\rightarrowOFC projection motifs that wire state representations to value-caching circuits; (iii) SWR-replay machinery for offline, prioritized value propagation; and (iv) the mPFC controllability-detection circuit for generating empowerment prediction errors. All four are phylogenetically conserved–the hippocampal formation is homologous across mammals (with antecedents in reptilian medial pallium), the mesolimbic dopamine system is ancient, and mPFC controllability circuitry appears shared across mammalian orders 8. The organism thus arrives equipped not with a pre-computed empowerment landscape but with the architectural scaffold to rapidly construct, cache, maintain, and update one through experience–converting a computationally prohibitive on-line optimization into an incrementally refined lookup.
